Alcaraz storms past world number one Zverev to win maiden ATP Finals title

Alcaraz joins an exclusive list, becoming one of only four men to have won all four majors and the ATP Finals.

Seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz powered past world number one Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (9-7) on Sunday to win his maiden ATP Finals title.

The Spaniard, who returned at the US Open after a four-month break due to a wrist injury, saved three set points in the tiebreak before completing his 14th consecutive victory and ending the year with a third straight title, having also triumphed in Vienna and Paris.

The 23-year-old, who is the youngest man to have completed the career Grand Slam, secured the biggest tour title that had eluded him after finishing runner-up at the ATP Finals last year.

Since losing in the quarterfinals of the 2026 US Open, he has won four titles with a 22-1 record.

“For me, it’s been an amazing week,” Alcaraz said. “I couldn’t have ended the week in a better way. I’m just really proud and really happy with everything I have done this week.

“I’ve been through really difficult moments within myself, with my team, and we went through everything playing great tennis. This trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time.

“It means the world to me.”

For Zverev, the defeat brought an end to his most successful season, in which he won his first two Grand Slam titles and rose to the top of the world rankings.

Alcaraz initially faced little resistance from a sluggish Zverev, who had not dropped a set en route to the final. The German struggled with his usually booming serve and made 19 unforced errors in the first set.

What had been billed as a blockbuster turned out to be a one-man show after Alcaraz bagged an early break to take control of the first set.

Zverev, a two-time ATP Finals champion, had saved all six break points he had faced during the group stage, but on Sunday he was struggling to keep pace with Alcaraz from the start.

The Spaniard earned five break points during the German’s first two service games, converting one of them. By the end of the fifth game, Zverev had racked up 15 unforced errors.

While the Spaniard buzzed around the court with his trademark intensity, chasing down every ball and nodding along to the music in the arena during the changeovers, Zverev looked sluggish and slow.

He earned one break back to cut Alcaraz’s lead to 4-2, but three points later his frustration boiled over when he argued with the umpire over a time violation warning.

The second set looked to be following a similar pattern, with Alcaraz keeping the level high and earning another early break.

But Zverev won three games on the trot to lead 5-4 and eventually forced a tiebreak. He could not convert any of his three consecutive set points, however, before Alcaraz clinched the win.

Alongside Roger Federer, Andre Agassi and Novak Djokovic, Alcaraz now forms part of an exclusive list of men to have won all four majors and the ATP Finals.

item.title: Is rule-breaking contagious? The bad apple effect explained
item.description:

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation

Rule-breaking is contagious – and good examples barely help

Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study finds, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a difference.

Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."

How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

Is rule-breaking contagious?

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Do good role models make people follow rules?

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?

To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

What does this mean in real life?

Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

As Syria-EU talks progress, diplomats fear focus will be on repatriation

Syria and the EU are in talks on trade and political ties, but migration will likely be the key issue of discussion.

Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiments in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following former President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with over a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But, they added, these affairs must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after war and decades of dictatorship.

“The migration issue is a big issue in Europe today,” Iyad Jaber, the Damascus-based Head of Middle East at Timios & Co and a former French diplomat of Syrian origin, told Al Jazeera. “Especially with right-wing and far-right wing [parties] taking more political space, it is moving political speech on migration.”

Deepening agreement

The first cooperation agreement between Europe and Syria was signed in 1978 by the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community (EEC), when Hafez al-Assad was Syria’s president. The agreement was focused on the economic and social development of Syria and a deepening of ties between the two parties.

In 2008, the EU-Syria Association Agreement was proposed but never signed by either side, largely due to concerns over the Assad government’s record on human rights. In 2011, when the government brutally repressed a popular uprising, the EU suspended ties with Syria.

During that time, the EU moved its diplomatic mission to Beirut and imposed sanctions on the Assad regime, freezing its assets and imposing travel bans on key officials.

Since the overthrow of the Assad regime, the EU has aimed to revive relations with the country. It lifted all economic sanctions on Syria last year, though some dual-use export controls and state institutions remain sanctioned.

In January, Brussels announced a two-year funding package of 620m euros ($680m) for Syria and in May the EU held its first high-level political dialogue with Syria, which aimed to revive bilateral relations.

The EU’s diplomatic service prepared a discussion paper outlining the normalisation efforts. Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

Kallas said diplomats are now working through technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create frameworks for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

Many European nations have been exploring reopening embassies or missions in Syria, diplomats told Al Jazeera, while Syrian and EU officials continue talks on normalisation and sanctions removal.

Syria’s European Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Sally Shobat, met the Head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the European External Action Service, Jonas Jonsson, on Saturday, after earlier holding bilateral meetings with French, Cypriot and Belgian diplomatic officials.

Priorities

Since the fall of the Assad government, Syria’s new government has worked to revive suspended relations and remove sanctions imposed on its predecessor. Many of the penalties have now been removed and relations with many countries, notably members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the United States, have also improved.

EU-Syrian relations may be moving in a positive direction, but experts said there are still many legal and technical obstacles to full normalisation.

“Every country has their own foreign policy,” Zakaria Al-Shmaly, a nonresident Fellow at TIMEP focusing on EU-Syria relations, told Al Jazeera.

Still, Syria has tried to prove its importance to Europe in security matters, particularly in the fight against ISIL and as an energy transit point following global disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Europe needs Syria as much as Syria needs Europe,” Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in Nicosia in April, after an informal meeting between Syria and EU officials.

In April, al-Sharaa proposed the Four Seas and Nine Corridors Initiative, a proposed transatlantic framework connecting the Gulf, Caspian Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea via a Syria–Turkiye pipeline and transit corridor. The proposal bypasses the Strait of Hormuz for a land pipeline through Syria, following disruptions to shipping because of the US-Israeli war on Iran which began in February.

“Every power is using Syria to undermine Iran,” Al-Shmaly said.

Another key point of discussion between the EU and Syria as normalisation talks continue will be trade. Experts said Brussels will likely try to open the Syrian market to EU products, which could benefit Syrian consumers by lowering costs on certain items. However, Syrian negotiators must also consider what kind of things Syrian companies can export to the EU.…

Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

The group, coordinated by the all-party group on anti-corruption (APPG), said an improvement in corporate transparency in the overseas territories was essential after “years of broken promises and missed deadlines from certain jurisdictions, and despite repeated commitments to ending secrecy”.

They said some territories such as Gibraltar, Montserrat and St Helena had successfully opened corporate registers to the public.

But they called out the British Virgin Islands, saying it “in particular continues to let the British family down”. They said the Cayman Islands has raised its search fees to “prohibitive levels”, and Turks and Caicos have introduced huge fines for disclosing information from the register which they said was “undermining the entire purpose of open registers”.

They said that persistent engagement in good faith from the UK government has yielded few results, in the face of “outright disregard for the will of parliament”.

The BVI has a register launched this year which allows people to apply for access to ownership information if they have a “legitimate interest” such as investigating money laundering. A BVI Government spokesperson said: “We are proud of the BVI’s Legitimate Interest Access register introduced earlier this year, which allows for prompt, proportionate access, in line with international standards.

“We continue to work closely with the UK Government, delivering a major governance and regulatory reform programme to support global efforts combatting illicit finance, enforcing sanctions and recovering criminal assets - with significant progress recently recognised by the Financial Action Task Force.”

However, ahead of the meeting, the MPs including former Conservative Foreign Office minister Andrew Mitchell and Labour anti-corruption expert Phil Brickell are asking Miliband to lay an order in council mandating fully public registers of beneficial ownership in jurisdictions that continue to fail to meet their obligations.

They said it was important for UK national security “because continued secrecy undermines our ability to enforce sanctions and leaves us open to hostile state actors and criminal networks”. Second, they said developing countries continue to be destabilised and looted by kleptocrats using Britain’s own offshore financial centres to clean and stash their ill-gotten gains.

Parliament voted for open registers in 2018 and the UK government had expected public access registers to be in place in all overseas territories and crown dependencies by 2023. However, this deadline was not met.

While an order in council to mandate open registers was drafted in 2020, the government said that because there were “firm commitments” from the overseas territories to introduce public registers, the order would not be used. It said it would keep this decision under review.

Brickell, Labour chair of the APPG, said “it should never have come to this but every year of deliberate delay is another year in which kleptocrats, tax dodgers and money launderers can hide behind a British flag”.

“That is a stain on the reputation of our global family. This joint ministerial council must be the moment we finally draw a line under it.”

Mitchell, a Conservative vice-chair of the APPG and former development secretary, said: “When parliament voted for public registers in 2018, it was not making a polite request. It was the clear, cross-party will of the House of Commons, and it should have been respected.

“Instead, money stolen from some of the poorest people on earth is still being hidden behind anonymous companies in British jurisdictions. That money should be building hospitals and schools. It is paying for yachts and mansions instead, and the price is measured in lives. The British family has been patient for long enough. The foreign secretary has the power to act, and I urge him to use it.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Security is the first duty of any government. Hostile states and malign actors can exploit opaque corporate structures like those in the British Virgin Islands to hide their assets and support activity that threatens our national security.

“Ministers are actively considering how best to ensure that, where the risks are greatest, law enforcement agencies have the information they need to progress critical investigations. We will continue ongoing engagement with Overseas Territories on these issues.”

Market regulators in South Korea, China and Taiwan have introduced new measures aimed at supporting markets, as a tech-fueled sell-off in the region spills into another week.

On Sunday, South Korea's finance ministry said it would prepare its securities-market stabilization fund for immediate activation. The fund, reportedly established in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic by financial firms and other institutions seeks to support markets during sharp downturns and is valued at 10.76 trillion won (nearly $8 billion).

The government also plans to relax listed companies' daily share-buyback order limits for three months, starting Nov. 24 and start a "special intensive monitoring period" to prevent illegal short-selling. Regulators will also track margin lending and forced liquidations.

South Korean stocks have seen wild swings over 2026 as investors piled into, then fled from its two tech heavyweights, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both critical companies in the AI supply chain. The benchmark Kospi index is deep in bear territory, down more than 46% from its June high.

The ministry said that it "assessed that volatility in domestic and international stock markets has significantly increased recently due to internal and external uncertainties surrounding the global AI and semiconductor industries, as well as U.S. interest rate hikes," according to a Google translation of the release in Korean.

However, Seoul also said that the mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact, and that "excessive anxiety is not a concern."

Taiwan, which is also exposed to the AI industry through Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and other tech firms, has also moved to rein in market volatility.

Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission announced Friday that short selling below the closing price was "completely prohibited," while making it an exception if used for hedging purposes by securities and futures firms.

"Investors must not sell listed (OTC) stocks or Taiwan Depositary Receipts at a price lower than the closing price of the previous trading day," the FSC said, according to a Google translation of the statement in Chinese.

Margin requirements for short selling will also be increased, and applications from securities firms to issue warrants for listing will be suspended, as the regulator aims to curb speculative activity.

In a similar move to Seoul, Taipei encouraged firms to buy back stocks, adding that the purchases will be included in the companies' environmental, social and governance scores if completed between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.

The island's stock market is heavily dominated by its tech industry, most notably, chip manufacturing giant TSMC. The stock fell 15% last week, while the index dropped 17.5%.

While South Korea and Taiwan are looking to curb speculative trading to arrest the slide in their markets, Beijing is looking to encourage more leverage-based buying.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange said on Sunday that exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed stock purchases to 80% from 100%, starting Nov. 30. That means investors will be able to borrow more for their stock market bets.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges also announced fee cuts, while Shenzhen proposed a market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board. The steps will help inject more liquidity into the market that has also born the brunt of the souring in tech and AI trade, with the benchmark CSI 300 index closing lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks.

Seoul's markets led losses in the region, with the Kospi down over 3.26%. Smaller losses were seen in mainland China's CSI 300, which declined 0.71%. The Taiwan Weighted Index, however, reversed earlier losses to gain over 2% on Monday.

New Zealand’s Mitchell, Phillips frustrate India as first Test ends in draw

New Zealand rescued a draw on the final day, surviving 120 overs in a fighting display to finish on 239-5 at the close.

New Zealand fought a rearguard action to deny India as the first Test in Wellington ended in a draw on Monday, with the tourists five wickets short of converting their mammoth first-innings lead into victory.

India entered the final day needing eight dismissals to take a 1-0 lead in the series and boost their World Test Championship (WTC) hopes, but New Zealand were down to their last two specialist batters at tea.

New Zealand were 239-5 in their second innings, still trailing India’s first-innings 720-9 declared by 113 runs, when the captains shook hands to end the contest.

Daryl Mitchell, who made 49 not out, and first-innings centurion Glenn Phillips (26) put on 63 for the sixth wicket on a Basin Reserve track that had been all but lifeless since the opening session and a bit of the match.

“I think we knew it was going to be a challenge to get 10 wickets on that wicket,” said India captain Shubman Gill.

“I didn’t really think having five or 10 extra overs would have helped that much. We also wanted to keep our bowlers fresh with the quick turnaround.”

India will take some confidence from their batting performance as they head to Christchurch for the second Test, starting on Friday, after six players each scored a half-century or better in a single innings.

KL Rahul (136) and Rishabh Pant (128) both hit centuries in contrasting styles, while Gill fell two runs short of the milestone.

Pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah impressed on his return to Test cricket after a year out, helping reduce New Zealand to 70-5 on the opening day, although he was used sparingly as India chased the result on Monday.

Phillips, Mitchell occupy the crease

New Zealand’s match was a tale of two sixth-wicket stands, the first of 216 runs between Henry Nicholls (175 not out) and Phillips (118) that enabled the hosts to post a respectable 368 in their first knock.

The second between Phillips and Mitchell on Monday was never going to be about the tally of runs but more about how long they occupied the crease.

“Throughout the week, we’ve had some guys put their hands up,” said New Zealand captain Tom Latham.

“Not just today but also throughout that first innings. We had our backs against the wall a little bit coming into that third innings, so to be in this position now, yeah, pretty pleased.”

Phillips and Mitchell came together in the sixth over after lunch when Tom Blundell departed for 15 off the bowling of Anshul Kamboj to leave New Zealand at 176-5.

The delivery appeared to have beaten the bat before going through to wicketkeeper Pant, but Kamboj heard something, and when India reviewed, the DRS technology revealed the faintest of nicks.

In the opening session, spinner Washington Sundar made the first breakthrough by removing Devon Conway for 65, the ball popping up off the opener’s bat and pad for Pant to collect with an athletic catch.

Rachin Ravindra, the other overnight batter, followed for 37 with a miscued shot off the bowling of seamer Prasidh Krishna that flew to Rahul in the slips.

India will rue a few missed chances to make further inroads into the New Zealand batting order, most notably a potential run-out that would have sent Mitchell back early in his innings.

The draw means New Zealand drop out of the top two in the 2025-27 WTC standings, with Australia moving up to join leaders and reigning champions South Africa. India remain fourth.

Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for about 30 people still missing.

Authorities were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.

Said Iqbal, a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the implementation of safety protocols was being assessed and that he would summon the factory’s chief executive.

Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.

She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.

The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.

“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”

He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.

Anxious relatives have waited for news outside the burnt-out factory.

The Banten province governor, Andra Soni, said an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

The firm employs about 5,000 people and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market. Its products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.

The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. He said the facility had adequate evacuation routes and fire protection systems that complied with applicable safety standards and were functioning at the time of the fire.

Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.

In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity

Sadie Harley

Senior Editor

Fifty-two million years ago, the Pacific tectonic plate began to slide under the Philippine Sea plate, forming the Mariana Trench, the deepest known valley on the Earth's ocean floor. The deepest part of this abyss, the Challenger Deep, is almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet) below sea level. But why is it so deep? Scientists trying to answer this question sent a remotely operated vehicle to collect samples around the Deep, where they found evidence of the world's deepest underwater explosive volcanic eruptions.

"Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised," said Dr. Robert J. Stern of the University of Texas at Dallas, lead author of an article in Frontiers in Earth Science. "These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean."

ROVing in the Deep

The researchers sailed to the Mariana Trench in late 2024 to deploy the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Jason/Medea. Although Jason/Medea can't dive deeper than 6,500 meters (21,300 feet) below sea level, this still allows it to sample the Deep's trench wall. They focused on a 550-kilometer-long (342-mile-long) forearc segment near the Challenger Deep.

Jason/Medea completed seven dives across an approximately 300-kilometer (186-mile) stretch of this forearc. These revealed that the eastern segment of the Deep is deeper, with steeper trench walls, but the boundary between Earth's crust and upper mantle lies closer to the surface than it does in the west. In the western segment, they found something astonishing: pyroclastic rocks from ultradeep volcanic eruptions.

The thin, flat layers of rock on the seabed are evidence of the deepest underwater volcanic eruption ever found. They're also in a totally unexpected place: the forearc is part of a tectonic boundary where the mantle underneath is generally not hot enough to melt, so young lavas are rare.

"The intense pressures at the depths at which these submarine volcanoes erupted make the eruption style different than it would be on land or in shallow water, where the pressures are much lower," said Stern. "The explosive eruptions observed on land cannot be as powerful under these high-pressure conditions because the gases in the magma cannot expand so much. We are still studying this phenomenon and trying to understand it."

6,500 meters (21,300 feet) under the sea

The team also concluded that the forearc is stretching from east to west along the seafloor, but the stretching happens differently at each end. In general, finding older rocks indicates that the segment is extending by mechanical stretching of the plates, like taffy being pulled apart, while finding younger volcanic rocks indicates that the segment is extending by adding magma from the mantle.

The scientists found more old rocks in the east and more young rocks in the west, suggesting that the eastern segment stretches mechanically while the western segment is accumulating magma. However, more sampling and radiometric dating are needed to test this hypothesis.

The scientists' work also supports our understanding of why the Challenger Deep is so deep. The two plates at the associated subduction zone are relatively weakly attached to each other, which allows the plate sliding underneath to move more easily. This plate is also narrow and short, which allows it to bend more tightly than normal as it sinks. The steeper dip increases the trench's depth.

"The sinking of oceanic plates in subduction zones provides most of the energy that makes Earth's tectonic plates move, so as this subduction zone widens, it will affect plate motions at least in the western Pacific," said Stern, explaining that as the forearc is stretching, the existing subduction zone must also widen.

The many surprises of the Challenger Deep make the team keen to return and sample more, to build a more complete picture of the world 6,500 meters (21,300 feet) under the sea. The Jason/Medea system doesn't allow them to go deeper.

"We haven't identified the eruption sites yet," said Stern. "We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don't think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to reweld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would've been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances."

"We would like to study more of the Challenger Deep forearc segment and go to greater depths," added Stern. "We were unable to study the seafloor between the depths of 6,500 meters (21,300 feet) and 11,000 meters (36,000 feet), the depth of the Challenger Deep. Only Chinese scientists and some wealthy entrepreneurs now have research tools capable of working down to the bottom of the Challenger Deep."

Impossible volcanic eruption spotted in deepest part of the ocean, perplexing scientists

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

The deepest place on Earth

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

New mysteries

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid — a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."…

Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

COP31 will not be remembered fondly.

The longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the hosts would be known as the "implementation COP".

The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:

- Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external

- The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life

- Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths â that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible â it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.

No money, more fossil fuels

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts â countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (Â£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

While the Russian delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

165 is the magic number

While the world's press and, it seems, many of the countries focused on the cover text, the central political agreement, at this year's talks there were 164 other items on the agenda for countries to discuss.

And some of those were agreed.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits â money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases â will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

The economics have been changing too.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive, and against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".…

Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench says they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, said in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”

Veteran robot still making discoveries 30 years on

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

The robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

In this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”

The unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well: the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

Researcher examines how blood vessel damage relates to memory loss

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Alzheimer's disease is often the focus when someone develops memory problems. But changes in the brain's blood vessels may also be part of the picture—and new research by the University of Kentucky's Cellas Hayes, Ph.D., helps explain why those changes deserve closer attention.

Hayes, an assistant professor who recently joined UK's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging, and his collaborators examined how different types of blood vessel damage relate to memory and thinking, and how much of those relationships could be explained by Alzheimer's-related brain changes.

Their findings, published in the journal Brain, point to an important distinction: While amyloid protein buildup in blood vessel walls was closely connected with Alzheimer's-related changes, thickening and hardening of the brain's small blood vessels remained linked to poorer thinking abilities even after researchers accounted for those changes.

"Different types of blood vessel damage may tell us different things about memory loss," Hayes said. "Understanding those differences could help researchers develop more complete approaches to dementia prevention and treatment."

Linking cognitive tests with brain examinations

The study used data from 1,269 people who participated in research at 34 Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs), including those at Sanders-Brown's ADRC. Participants completed tests of memory and thinking during their lives and donated their brains for examination after death. Their average age at death was 84.

Researchers compared participants' most recent test results with findings from their brain examinations. The tests assessed memory, the ability to use and understand words, and skills such as planning and problem-solving.

The team examined five types of blood vessel damage, including thickened small vessels, fatty deposits in larger arteries, protein buildup in vessel walls and areas of brain tissue damaged by interrupted blood flow. Their analyses accounted for differences in age, sex, education and a genetic factor associated with Alzheimer's risk.

Two vessel conditions show different patterns

Two forms of vessel disease stood out.

The first, called arteriolosclerosis, involves thickening and hardening of the brain's small blood vessels. About 41% of participants had moderate or severe changes of this type.

More severe small-vessel thickening was associated with poorer performance in memory, language, and planning and problem-solving. Although Alzheimer's-related changes explained part of those relationships in the researchers' statistical models, a substantial connection remained after those changes were taken into account.

"Blood vessel health is an important part of understanding memory loss," Hayes said. "In our study, damage to the brain's small blood vessels was linked to poorer memory and thinking even after accounting for Alzheimer's-related changes."

The second condition, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, occurs when amyloid protein builds up in blood vessel walls. About 56% of participants had these deposits.

Greater severity of this condition was also associated with poorer performance across all three thinking abilities. However, Alzheimer's-related changes accounted for a much larger share of those relationships—roughly 60% to 90%, depending on the thinking ability measured. These estimates describe relationships within the study's statistical models, rather than an individual person's risk of dementia.

Treatments may need to address multiple contributors

Together, the findings help distinguish conditions that often occur in the same brain but may have different relationships with memory and thinking.

That distinction could help guide future research into treatments that address several contributors to cognitive problems. Therapies focused on Alzheimer's-related changes alone may leave other sources of difficulty unaddressed, including changes to the vessels and blood flow in the brain.

"To develop more complete approaches to dementia, we need to understand the multiple types of damage that can occur in the same brain," Hayes said. "An important next question is whether addressing blood vessel disease alongside Alzheimer's-related changes can better preserve memory and thinking."

Causation and broader applicability remain uncertain

The study does not establish that blood vessel damage causes Alzheimer's disease or that treating it will prevent memory loss. Because the brain conditions were examined together after death, researchers could not determine which developed first.

The participants also represented a selected research population: Approximately 95% were white, their average education was 16 years and about 60% had dementia at their last assessment. Further studies are needed to determine whether the same patterns appear in more diverse populations.

Following people over time, while measuring blood vessel changes, Alzheimer's markers and thinking abilities, will be an important next step.

The findings connect with broader work underway in Hayes' laboratory at Sanders-Brown and UK's Department of Neuroscience. His team studies how blood markers of Alzheimer's disease and other brain changes evolve over time, alongside genetic research and investigations into how vascular health and social factors contribute to differences in brain aging. The goal is to identify opportunities to reduce risk, slow disease progression and develop more personalized approaches to care.

Hayes also emphasized the contributions of research participants and their families, whose decisions to donate made the study possible.

"Brain donation provides an extraordinary opportunity to understand what underlies memory and thinking problems," Hayes said. "This work reflects the generosity of participants and families who wanted to help future generations."

Several prior studies confirmed that parental tobacco and e-cigarette use is a strong predictor of adolescent use. What was less known was whether the use of tobacco or e-cigarettes among parents and caregivers was associated with broader adolescent substance use.

Understanding the associations between household tobacco and e-cigarette use and teen substance use could help address risks related to adolescent tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and other substance use.

To help address this knowledge gap, researchers linked two sources of information already collected in the electronic health record (EHR) during routine visits across CHOP's Care Network between January 2025 and May 2026: parents' and caregivers' answers to tobacco screening questions from an automated tobacco treatment program, and adolescents' own answers on a confidential health questionnaire.

Rather than focus solely on tobacco and e-cigarette use, researchers explored whether adolescents were more likely to use other substances and potentially develop patterns of high-risk use, as measured by a validated adolescent screening tool.

"This study shows that household tobacco and e-cigarette use isn't just a parental health issue. It's a risk factor for adolescent substance use that pediatric clinicians can act on," said lead study author Brian Jenssen, MD, MSHP, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, a primary care pediatrician and medical director for value-based care for the CHOP Care Network, and associate director for clinical impact at Clinical Futures at CHOP.

The study analyzed data from 60,069 adolescents and found that nearly 1 in 4 adolescents (23.5%) used tobacco or nicotine products when both the parent or caregiver at the visit and another adult in the home used tobacco or e-cigarettes, compared with 13.5% when only the parent or caregiver used, 11.8% when only another adult in the home used and 2.0% when no one in the home used.

Similar patterns were observed with alcohol, marijuana and other substances. After accounting for age, sex, insurance and neighborhood opportunity, adolescents in homes where both a parent and another adult used tobacco or e-cigarettes had nearly 15 times the odds of screening positive for high-risk substance use as adolescents in homes with no use.

This pattern held across most substances.

Because the study captured data at a single point in time, it cannot establish that household tobacco or e-cigarette use causes adolescent substance use; shared family, social and environmental factors may also play a role. Still, the consistent pattern across substances suggests household use is a practical risk signal for pediatric clinicians.

The EHR-integrated screening system that generated these data is currently used across CHOP, including all 31 CHOP Care Network practices, multiple subspecialty sites and both emergency departments. A parent's positive tobacco screen can trigger cessation support for the parent and alert clinicians to provide targeted substance-use prevention for the adolescent—addressing risk across two generations in a single visit.

"Every time a parent comes in for their child's checkup, we have an opportunity to protect not just one patient, but the whole family," Jenssen said. "This study shows we can use the data we already have to do exactly that."

Why it is here: Significant public health trend with clear reporting and useful context

Daily cannabis use surpasses daily drinking among Canadians under 50, survey finds

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Six years after cannabis legalization, more adults under 50 in Canada use cannabis daily than drink every day, and daily cannabis smoking is now as common as daily cigarette smoking for adults under age 35, according to new research in CMAJ (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

"These shifts likely have profound implications for mental health, heart disease and lung health, and cancer risk that we are only beginning to understand," says Dr. Daniel Myran, the senior author, who is the Cheesbrough Research Chair at North York General, a clinician-scientist and associate professor at the University of Toronto's Department of Family and Community Medicine, and a scientist at ICES and the Bruyère Health Research Institute.

Over the last 20 years, cannabis use has increased in Canada and the United States, tobacco use has declined, and alcohol use has remained stable or declined in some groups. Canada legalized nonmedical cannabis in 2018, becoming the first country in the world to allow commercial retail sales and promotion.

In 2020, a wide variety of products with high tetrahydrocannabinol content, including vapes, edibles and concentrates, entered the legal market. While adolescent cannabis use has remained largely stable after legalization—though at some of the highest levels in the world—regular cannabis use has increased in adults.

Regular cannabis use has long been associated with addiction, psychosis and schizophrenia. Increasing evidence suggests it may be a risk factor for chronic disease, including heart attacks, strokes, lung disease and other mental health problems, and evidence is limited and mixed on cancer risk.

In this study, researchers looked at daily use of cannabis, alcohol and tobacco reported from almost 100,000 respondents to the 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS).

Many previous studies have examined changes in cannabis use over time and have primarily looked at past-year use. This study examined daily use, a much stronger predictor of mental health and addiction. It also examined cannabis by mode of use and compared it to the regular use of other substances.

"This study suggests a generational shift in substance use behaviors has taken place, which will likely have long-term implications for population health," says lead author Dr. André McDonald, a psychiatric epidemiologist and Canadian Institutes of Health Research postdoctoral fellow at McMaster University's Peter Boris Center for Addictions Research, Hamilton, Ontario.

"Declining cigarette use among younger people reflects long-term tobacco-control policies, changing social norms and greater awareness of harms. Conversely, increases in cannabis use are consistent with greater availability, social acceptability and normalization in the postlegalization era."

"One of the most surprising findings was that a substantial number of people who use cannabis daily don't drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes every day," says Myran.

"Only 11.2% of people who use cannabis daily also drink alcohol daily, while only 38.4% also smoke cigarettes daily. It is commonly assumed that regular cannabis smoking goes hand in hand with tobacco use, but that didn't appear to be the case for almost two-thirds of people who use cannabis daily."

Effect of legalization

"Canada is the first country in the world to create a commercial retail market with a wide variety of product offerings and product promotion. To me, many of the patterns of cannabis use that are emerging in Canada's mature legal market offer a strong caution to other countries around the world about the potential harms of this approach," says Myran.

"One of the arguments for legalization and increasing the variety of products on the market is that it would shift people away from smoked cannabis toward other forms of use, like edibles, that may have lower risk for heart or lung disease or cancer. These findings don't really support that occurring; in people who use cannabis daily, 68% continue to report smoking as the main method of use."

Cannabis legalization had a major impact on consumption patterns, with 41% of adults who used cannabis daily reporting they began doing so after legalization. More than half of females using cannabis daily (51.2%) reported starting daily cannabis use after legalization. This proportion was 85.4% for younger adults (ages 18 to 24 years) using cannabis daily.

"Policy efforts have historically focused on reducing alcohol and tobacco use, and for good reason. Our findings suggest high-frequency cannabis use needs to be considered a priority alongside them. Over 1.8 million Canadians now use cannabis daily, of whom 750,000 began doing so after legalization. Given the health risks involved, preventing and reducing cannabis use has become a pressing public health issue," adds McDonald.

In places like Canada where cannabis is legal, the authors suggest tactics such as stronger communications about risk, marketing and retail restrictions, an increased minimum legal age, and targeted prevention and harm-reduction strategies to reduce usage in younger adults and vulnerable populations.

Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out

- Published

Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.

"Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment."

Gilbert told the BBC there was a "huge shortfall" in radiologists and that the number of imaging examinations was increasing by 8% a year.

Screening 'saved my life'

Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.

She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.

She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms."

Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.

"I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.

How will the trial work?

Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.

The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.

Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.

Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.

In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts. In another, it will review images afterwards.

The Â£11m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.

'Huge potential'

On a visit to the breast screening unit at Addenbrooke's Hospital, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper told the BBC: "AI has huge potential to improve treatment, which is why we need trials like this to ensure we are using it in the most effective way with proper safeguards."

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said NHS breast screening "saves lives" and he urged every woman invited to the trial to take part.

"Every scan will still be seen by a specialist, and if proven effective, it could ensure women get the diagnosis and treatment they need sooner," he said.

Four AI companies are involved in the trial, which is expected to last around three years.

item.title: PageSift 1.7 "Resolve": Stop Trusting Retrieved Text — Verify the Conclusion
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

PageSift is a Rust web-content engine for LLM pipelines (305 stars, Apache-2.0). Version 1.7, released today, adds the layer that was still missing — checking the conclusions you draw from that text.

The problem: nobody verifies the answer

A retrieval pipeline hands text to a model. The model states conclusions: "the price is $42 a year", "it ships in March", "this tool causes fewer support tickets". Those sentences go into answers, reports, and databases. Nobody checks them.

And they rot. The price changes next month. Two sources disagree and the pipeline keeps whichever it read last. A press release gets copied by five sites and starts to look like five independent confirmations. A study that found a correlation gets quoted as proof of causation. Last year's price gets repeated as today's.

Scraping got the text back. Context (1.6) made the text traceable. The conclusion drawn from it was still taken on faith. Resolve is the layer that checks it.

One scenario, end to end

Say you monitor a product's price. The vendor's page says Widget Pro costs $42 per year. A reseller lists the same product at $45 per year. Your pipeline produces the sentence "Widget Pro costs $42 per year" and you ask Resolve to check it against the stored evidence.

The verdict is conflicted. Resolve tracks support and refutation as separate facts instead of averaging them into a score: one independent source supports the sentence, another independent source refutes it, and the record says exactly that, with citations to both.

Two weeks later the vendor raises the price to $50. The stored conclusion is not left standing. When the underlying evidence changes, Resolve re-checks only the conclusions that depend on the changed passages — and this one flips to refuted, with its full revision history preserved. A conclusion in Resolve is not a one-time judgment. It is a maintained object that stays answerable to its evidence.

The four ideas

1. A conclusion is a stored, versioned record. Each checked answer becomes a ConclusionRecord with one of nine states — supported, supported with qualifiers, refuted, conflicted, insufficient, temporal mismatch, causally unidentifiable, needs human review, observation degraded. Two of those states deserve emphasis: insufficient ("the evidence does not settle this") and causally unidentifiable ("the evidence shows correlation, not causation"). The system is allowed to say it cannot tell, and it does.

2. Checking is deterministic, in seven layers. The checker anchors every claim to its subject, so one product's price can never "confirm" another's. It keeps two time axes apart: when a page was observed versus the period the fact is valid for — a 2024 price cannot confirm a claim about today. It normalizes quantities, currencies, and billing periods, so $42 per month does not confirm $42 per year. It guards negation and dropped qualifiers ("does not include shipping" refutes "includes shipping"; an omitted "unless" downgrades a claim to qualified instead of supported). It refuses causal language on correlational evidence. It collapses copied sources that share one origin, so a syndicated reprint counts once, not five times. And it verifies that every citation actually reaches the passage it claims to support.

3. It argues against itself. After a check, Resolve runs a counter-search: it actively looks for errata, exceptions, and contradicting records that would overturn the conclusion, and attaches an audit of what it searched. The audit states its own limit in plain terms — in an open world, finding no counter-evidence is not proof. Absence of evidence is recorded as absence, never converted into confidence.

4. Conclusions are maintained, not just made. When sources change, an incremental reconciliation finds the affected conclusions and re-verifies only those, cutting off early when a change is a pure relocation or a reconfirmation. In the release evaluation this ran 4.47× faster than full re-verification — which is what makes it practical to re-check every stored conclusion every time its evidence moves, instead of auditing samples once in a while.

What the evaluation says

The release ships an adversarial evaluation set of 64 cases built to fool a checker: mirror copies, stale prices, billing-period swaps, negation traps, causal overreach. A keyword-overlap baseline — "the words appear in the source, so the claim is supported" — produced a false-support rate of 0.8333. It blessed five out of six wrong answers. Resolve's false-support rate on the same set was 0.0000, with supported precision and recall both at 1.0. In the mirror test, naive source counting gave false support at a rate of 1.0; after origin collapse, 0.

The core check runs at 9,448 checks per second (p50 96µs) on the benchmark machine. That number matters for one reason: verification this cheap does not have to be a nightly audit. It can run on every answer, at the moment the answer is produced.

One honest limitation, from the same evaluation: in deterministic mode, Resolve abstains on heavily metaphorical paraphrases — 3 out of 3 cases came back insufficient, with zero false supports. It would rather say "cannot tell" than guess at what a metaphor means. An optional hybrid mode lets a configured LLM judge those leftovers, but only with verbatim quote grounding, and it can never override a deterministic refutation.

When to use it, when not to

Use Resolve when a conclusion has to stay true: price and spec monitoring, answer auditing for RAG and agent systems, research claims you keep citing, any pipeline where a wrong sentence costs more than the check does.…

item.description:
