Why it is here: author interview, insight into writing process

If you ever find yourself in an airport newsagent, it might be worth peering inside one of Liz Pichon’s books. “I do guerrilla signings,” she tells me conspiratorially. “They let me go in and I sign all the books, just in case. I love the idea of kids buying a book, going on holiday and seeing that I’ve signed it. Sometimes I write ‘surprise!’”

It’s a wonder that she hasn’t got sore hands. Pichon is one of the UK’s foremost children’s authors, and this is a big year for her. Not only has she just published the 25th book in her Tom Gates series, Tom Gates Is Not Famous (Yet), but this is the 15th anniversary of the first instalment. She has, at last count, sold 16.5m books in 47 languages, and her work has been adapted for both stage and screen.

“I can’t believe it’s 15 years since the first one came out,” she says on a video call from her home. “Now I get 19- and 20-year-olds that grew up with my books. They’ll turn up at an event with a big stack of them and go ‘these were my favourites’, which makes me feel very old.”

Although by no means Pichon’s only project – her comic book series The Mubbles is going from strength to strength – Tom Gates seems more and more like her life’s work. A decade and a half is a long time to maintain any series, let alone one in which the main character has been at the same school all along. But the magic of Tom Gates is that the books never feel as if they’re covering old ground. The stories (usually about Tom’s scrapes with his best friend, Derek, older sister Delia and irritating classmate Marcus Meldrew) remain fresh, while the presentation – scrappy, handmade, packed with bonus content and extra features – is just as endearing as ever.

“There’s always that moment of slight panic when you first start, where you think: ‘What am I going to write about this time? What haven’t I covered?’” she says. “But I write about small details of family life, things that might happen at home and school, with friends and pets. There’s always something that comes up.”

The newest book is based on something that once happened to her husband, songwriter and producer Mark Flannery, who spent his early career as a studio runner for U2. “He told me a story about how he was trying to go to a Simple Minds concert with a friend and they couldn’t get in,” she says. “All of a sudden this big limo pulls up, and U2 get out. The drummer goes, ‘Mark come with us, we’ll get you in.’ I always thought that would be a fun plot for a book.”

Pichon enjoys a weird kind of success. Unlike those who write for adults, whose readers might stay with them for a lifetime, children’s authors only have their followers for a short stretch before they grow up and move on. As such, Tom Gates has managed to entertain a rolling caravan of new fans, which is astoundingly hard to maintain. Pichon puts this down to her refusal to cater to modern tastes.

“There’s not much technology,” she explains. “You won’t get much text messaging or anything like that. There are some things in childhood that just don’t change. Sibling rivalries, stuff like that. Children in different territories enjoy reading these books, and I think maybe one reason is because I’m not very specific, so they can really put themselves into the setting.”

Now 63, Pichon grew up in London and lives in Brighton. She didn’t start writing until she was in her mid-40s, having previously worked designing album covers for Jive Records and a range of greetings cards, and then illustrating picture books for other writers. The late start is something she puts down to insecurity over her dyslexia as a child. “I came from a generation where people just thought I wasn’t academic,” she says. “Of all the things I was good at, none of them were considered to be things you could actually make a living from. So you grow up with that in the background, a lack of expectation. I didn’t have a clue what I wanted to do.”

Tom Gates came from what she describes as a desire to start making things she was genuinely proud of. The first was created in an exercise book, full of handwritten diary-style text and visuals. “I took all the things I’d learned in picture books, like grabby page turns, and used them for a slightly older audience,” she says. The result was her signature style with ideas tumbling out in sketches, sight gags and bonus content. (The latest contains a short script that readers can act out with their friends, and songs she has written for the book can be found on streaming platforms.) “Kids get into the stories really quickly because the presentation is so accessible,” she says.

“I’m passionate about this,” Pichon continues. “When I do school visits, we talk about things that are happening in the kids’ lives, and how they can get those stories out of their heads. I show them how I tell stories with drawings and doodles and things. Hopefully when they leave, they’re not only excited about reading the books, but actually going on to be creative themselves. We all tell stories in different ways. Some kids will feel like they can’t draw, or can’t write, or aren’t very good at spelling, and this gives them a way to feel like they’re being seen and heard and celebrated.”

A core part of Pichon’s audience is what some would dub “reluctant readers”, although she prefers the term “unconfident”; youngsters who need a visual element to suck them into a story. “They just need a book that gets them in,” she says. “Once they’re in, they’re readers.” The visuals of Pichon’s books – plus the fact that they’re incredibly funny, and can be read for pure enjoyment – have meant that she has amassed something of a rarity in these times; an audience largely composed of boys.…

item.description:

Why it is here: biographical overview, cultural significance

John Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.”

I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole.

There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”.

The entry point

Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics.

The prizewinner

The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972). The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him.

The quiet masterpiece

Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years.

The one for writers

One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists.

The one for artists

Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery.

The best on photography

Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and those who are using the photography are often contradictory”.

The best on politics

To some extent, everything Berger wrote was political; he was always concerned with the human experience in relation to society. One topic he wrote about repeatedly was migration, most memorably in A Seventh Man (1975), another remarkable collaboration with Mohr. This galvanising book intimately documents the experience of migrant labourers seeking work in western Europe in the early 1970s, but it remains soberingly topical today.

The one that will make you cry

G. may have won the Booker prize, but To the Wedding (1995) is Berger’s greatest novel. Through fragments of conversations, songs and silences, we follow a mother and father, estranged for many years, travelling across Europe to the wedding of their daughter Ninon. It’s both a heartbreaking story and a triumphantly optimistic celebration of love and life. Colum McCann calls it “one of the greatest and most honest love stories of our time.”

The one that deserves more attention

The wonderful Here Is Where We Meet (2005) is fiction – or is it? In 8½ chapters, “John” has a series of encounters with people who are dead: he meets his mother sitting on a park bench in Lisbon, he meets his childhood mentor in Krakow market, he stands above the grave of Jorge Luis Borges in Geneva. This is Berger at his most playful, seamlessly blending novel, essay, criticism, memoir and travelogue. It’s a brilliant, unclassifiable achievement.

The one to carry in your pocket…

Why it is here: news report, relevant to literature

Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

According to a report in the Observer, Cooper, who died last October, committed “what appears to be extensive and deliberate plagiarism” by lifting at least 35 passages from The Serial alone.

McFadden’s daughter, Caroline McFadden, told the publication: “To steal her work so extensively and to profit off it is unconscionable.”

She said she was considering legal action, saying: “It absolutely boils my blood to think of someone stealing my mother’s work because I know how hard she worked at her craft.

“I will be looking at legal options as this can’t be allowed to stand. I sincerely hope that all of Dame Cooper’s work will be scrutinised to see if this was a pattern of hers and other talented authors’ work stolen.”

Cooper, who has sold more than 11m copies of her books in the UK alone, was given a damehood in the 2024 new year honours list for her services to literature and charity.

Disney+ is currently airing the second series of Rivals, the award-winning television adaptation of her most famous work. The show combines TV industry intrigue and racy sex scenes against the backdrop of the Cotswolds countryside in the fictional guise of Rutshire.

In its investigation, the Observer detailed 15 allegedly plagiarised passages from The Serial, which was first published from late 1975 as a weekly serialisation in a US newspaper before it was released as a book in May 1977.

In The Serial, McFadden, who died in 2024, created the off-and-on-again couple Kate and Harvey Holroyd, two progressives in California’s Marin County. The Observer noted several similarities with the dialogue in Cooper’s character, Berenice, an American feminist.

In The Serial, Kate says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open, loving relationship, based on growth and trust and sharing, and Harvey wanted his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we just weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

In Prudence, Berenice says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open living relationship based on trust and growth, and all he wanted was his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

The publication also cited another example from The Serial in which Harvey was offered lifestyle advice. The passage said: “Cut out the nine-to-five shit, Harv. You gotta get in touch with the universe. That’s the first step.”

In Prudence, Berenice offered similar advice. “You ought to cut out that nine to five shit … And get in touch with the universe.”

The Observer said it began looking at Prudence after a reader pointed out similarities with a scene in Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair.

The publication alleged that Cooper “lifts directly” from chapter 22 of the novel “both in narrative architecture and in line-by-line choice of words”. Tey died in 1952 and left no heirs.

Cooper is said to have praised The Serial for its parody of the modern feminist in a 1982 Mail on Sunday column. She said she was “tremendously comforted” when she “came across a passage in the novel The Serial by Cyra McFadden, a marvellously funny send-up of American trendies in the late seventies”.

An inquest held last year concluded that Cooper suffered a fatal head injury in a fall at her Gloucestershire home. She was found by family on 4 October 2025 and died in hospital the following day.

The Guardian has contacted Cooper’s agent, Felicity Blunt at Curtis Brown, and her publisher, Penguin, for comment. The Observer said both had declined to provide a comment.

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.

As someone who was a child carer for my profoundly autistic brother, this thought – that caring is something that unites us as human beings – is one I find comforting. This unspoken, hidden and often unwritten club is one that took me a long time to realise existed, simply because when you are little, most of your peers aren’t doing care work yet (and the ones who are might not talk about it). You also don’t necessarily see it as care because to you the tasks just feel normal: making their tea or helping them go to the toilet is simply a part of loving that person. Yet, having that level of responsibility as a child can feel very lonely, because you are a child with adult responsibilities who has had to grow up far too quickly. At the time you don’t realise that getting older means the size of this “club” keeps expanding. Now I am in my 30s and, having seen what life has thrown at the people I know and love, and their families, I understand that caring is less exceptional than it used to feel.

I recently contributed to an anthology for supporters of the Carers Trust called Lives Less Seen: Untold Stories from Those Who Care. Among the contributions are several from young carers. Oliver writes about looking after his mum, who had a stroke four years ago, and how being put in touch with the trust’s young carers network and campaigning politically for the rights of children like him has made him feel not only less alone but proud to be a young carer. Like the all-party parliamentary group that Oliver has attended, I’d like to see improved attempts to identify young carers, whose education, wellbeing and future prospects are all impacted by their roles, and better, earlier support for them, including when they transition to adulthood.

Caring is so often thankless, and its role in keeping society afloat is so often underestimated, that learning to feel pride in it is crucial.

The anthology also contains moving drawings from the Honeypot Children’s Charity, which supports young carers and children aged five to 12. Being put in touch with other child carers and being encouraged to creatively process their feelings must make such a difference. I rejected groups like these when I was young, I think from a mixture of pride and fear. In retrospect I think such initiatives would have really helped me make sense of what my home life involved. For a long time, I was so allergic to the idea that people may feel sorry for me that I had emotionally blocked off the possibility of ever feeling compassion for myself. I think a lot of carers do this, especially when they are in survival mode. It’s very easy to view being sad about it as something self-indulgent and unproductive, especially when you feel you’re not suffering anywhere near as much as the person you’re caring for, and so it’s easier to put your feelings in a box.

My own contribution to the anthology is a letter to my younger self, but really it is for all child carers. I wanted someone in my position to know how much I regretted not seeking support at the time. “There is great comfort to be had in community and solidarity,” I write. “Other people save us. Dealing with family illness or disability can be so hard, but the compensation is that often, along the way, you get to meet some of the best people ever.”

Caring is one of the hardest and one of the most life-affirming things I have done with my time on this planet. Unpaid carers might feel unseen, unappreciated and ignored by successive governments, but I do think those of us who care or who have cared share a common compassion, understanding and sense of humour that can be immensely comforting when it’s tapped into. That, at least, is something to be celebrated as we continue to campaign for better lives for all carers.

- Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

There was positive progress on food and drink trade, youth mobility and aligning carbon markets. Yet there was also an inability to resolve relatively simple issues such as the fees young Europeans will pay to study at British universities from 2030, and whether the UK will apply the same tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the EU. That is a taste of what lies ahead if a future government, backed by a groundswell of public opinion, decides to apply to rejoin.

The fundamental problems of being outside the EU were laid bare: you have to pay for market access and align with rules on which you no longer have a vote. But the issues around seeking renewed membership were also highlighted: the EU always has the upper hand in accession negotiations and the candidate country must adopt its rulebook wholesale – including the free movement of people – and pay into the common budget.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, was right to say the door is always open but at a price. Burnham is right to argue that Brexit has not benefited the economy, ordinary people or the UK’s standing in the world. However you do the counterfactual economics, Britain has lost substantial investment, export markets and potential growth, while citizens have faced increasing hassle travelling and living on both sides of the Channel. Young people have also been robbed of opportunities to study and work abroad. As the EU’s divorce negotiator, Michel Barnier, accurately forecast, Brexit has been a lose-lose equation for both sides.

However, the summit also illustrated that the toxic British politics around any move to rejoin have not gone away. Once again, the issue would dominate the agenda if the choice were put to a referendum or made the centrepiece of the next general election.

Burnham is correct to reopen a national debate on the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU and to put the option of membership back on the table. As ever, there is a domestic political calculation in his gamble. It helps Labour win back voters lost to the Greens and the Liberal Democrats in this year’s local elections and to mobilise pro-European youth support. He may also reckon that working-class voters lost to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK care more about cost of living issues than they do about Europe.

Farage, who built his career on stoking English nationalism and conflating EU membership with uncontrolled immigration, was quick to warn of a betrayal of the British people’s democratic 2016 vote by political elites. The line of the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, that Burnham had been made to accept an unfair deal, in which the UK will have to pay too much for too little return, was a telling indicator of the epic battles over money that lie ahead.

Signals from Brussels before the summit suggested the EU would probably not insist that the UK join the euro or the Schengen area of passport-free travel. But it was equally clear that Margaret Thatcher’s EU budget rebate, won after an epic battle in 1984, would not be returning.

It’s not clear that the UK’s political class or its powerful Treasury mandarins have accepted the fundamental pay-to-play logic of either partial access to the EU market or full membership. The widely held denial that Britain needs to pay for market access led to the collapse of negotiations last year to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme of soft loans for joint defence projects. Brussels shares responsibility for that failure by pitching an unrealistically high entry fee.

While many EU countries would welcome the UK back for geopolitical as well as economic reasons, especially in northern and central Europe, it is less clear that France, which since the presidency of Charles de Gaulle has seen Britain as aligned with US interests, would be so keen. If the hard-right nationalist Marine Le Pen, who applauded Brexit, wins next year’s French presidential election, she has vowed to reduce Paris’s contribution to EU coffers and may want to charge London a high price.

The prospect of an EU in which hard-right national populists, less supportive of Ukraine and more friendly in some cases towards Russia, enjoy growing influence may also make rejoining less politically attractive to a UK that is trying to shake off a decade of its own national populism.

I would love to see the UK back in the EU, where it always belonged as a European nation. But I’m not sure I will see it in my lifetime.

- Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation of risks

The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa in mid-November when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition plant, explosions that are expected to send a plume of lead particles – a neurotoxin – over homes and farmland for miles. Late on Nov. 22, 2026, the Army announced the rescheduled date: Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving.

According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. Intentionally detonating the barrels is the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

In Middletown, a community of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa, news reports described people taping windows to prepare for the blast and covering air conditioners with tarps to keep lead out. Communities and state politicians didn’t learn about the plan until a few days before Nov. 20, when the detonations were initially planned. A federal court paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit after two groups sued, but the U.S. Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.

What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?

Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southwest. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead.

That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.

What can people do to stay safe in those areas?

Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.

Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.

Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, thought-provoking analysis

Listen to this essay

26 minute listen

The idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange. After all, governments must keep themselves informed and inform their citizens. That’s why they turn to the science of meteorology to predict weather patterns, to economics to understand patterns of growth and decline, and to the medical sciences to improve public health. So why wouldn’t governments also keep close alliances with religious institutions to know what’s going on with God?

Separating church and state appears strange from other perspectives as well. In the historical sweep of large-scale human societies, it’s a relative newcomer, often associated with the United States’ founding father Thomas Jefferson. In 1802, Jefferson asserted the principle of separation in a letter to the Danbury Baptist Association in Connecticut:

Believing with you that religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God … that the legitimate powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions, I contemplate with sovereign reverence that act of the whole American people which declared that their legislature would ‘make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof,’ thus building a wall of separation between Church and State.

We’re fans of Jefferson’s principle, one of us (Neil Van Leeuwen) being a philosophy professor who grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, and the other (Jacob Eisler) being a law professor who regularly attends synagogue. But Jefferson’s letter makes putting the principle into practice sound simpler than it is – as though governments could be entirely hands-off when it comes to people’s beliefs, or ‘opinions’. That, however, can’t be right: engaging with and shaping political, social and other kinds of beliefs is actually a core function of government. Public education guides what people believe about everything from mathematics to history to astronomy. Governments also shape beliefs for policy reasons. If fire department officials learn that people believe a building is safe when it isn’t, they will try to change what people believe about the building’s safety. Belief is also a category of legal interest. If a psychotherapist, for example, believes a patient is a danger to himself or others, the therapist is obligated by law to report that belief.

All this means that Jefferson’s ‘wall of separation’ can’t sensibly prohibit governments from intervening on beliefs of any type whatsoever. Rather, Jefferson – along with advocates of the principle who came after him – must have presupposed that there is something distinctive about religious beliefs that makes it reasonable to give them a different legal status.

But what is this distinctive thing? Is it that religious beliefs concern God? No, because Buddhism is a religion with its own beliefs, yet Buddhism has no supreme deity. Is it that religious beliefs concern the supernatural generally? No, because many superstitions that aren’t part of a religion concern the supernatural too. Is it that religious beliefs concern morality, as the biologist Stephen Jay Gould once suggested? No, because many religious beliefs aren’t about morality, and many moral beliefs aren’t religious. In any case, any system of government must presuppose some moral beliefs – eg, that murder is wrong – to be a government at all. These considerations might make one despair of articulating the psychological distinction of interest – what’s different about religious ‘belief’? – that’s needed to make sense of separating church and state in the first place.

Such attempts at characterising religious belief fail, we think, because they focus on belief contents, or what the believing is about. But since any given idea can be believed in a religious way or not, that won’t work. Our suggestion, then, is that religiously believing is a different attitude from ordinary matter-of-fact believing – a different way of relating to ideas – and that this is what’s distinctive about religious belief. In other words, sacralising an idea is different from just taking it to describe how things are. Furthermore, empirical research in cognitive science and anthropology of religion, along with accompanying philosophical analysis, can help reveal characteristic features of the difference in attitude we’re after. To have specific terms, we call that the difference between religious credence and factual belief. Understanding this difference, we’ll see, helps make sense of Jefferson’s wall of separation, and supports the rationale for separating church and state in liberal democracies more generally.

Whatever they are, ‘beliefs’ come in different varieties. The word ‘belief’ is polysemous – meaning it can refer to a range of different-but-related things – and it subsumes a motley crew: from humdrum factual beliefs (say, about where the ice-cream store is) to superstitions (like those found in astrology), and from moral beliefs about murder to philosophical beliefs about how ‘all is one’. As mentioned earlier, beliefs can also be categorised by their contents (what is the belief about? Is it about politics? Or maybe about a probable scientific theory?) Or by the attitude they embody (how does a person relate to given ideas or contents?) Here, however, we focus on the differences between matter-of-fact believing and religious credence as distinct ways in which people process ideas. There are, of course, more varieties of belief-like attitudes. But we home in on factual belief and religious credence since the differences in those attitudes matter most to the psychology of separating church and state.…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, informative on China's economic growth

This is our fourth article from Issue 26, which arrives with print subscribers this week.

Imagine if Y Combinator owned and ran San Francisco. Too much traffic? That’s bad for business. Highway 101 would be triple- or quadruple-deckered, and the metropolitan area might have a dozen subway lines, more like Madrid’s or Osaka’s networks than the BART as it stands. Heritage buildings? They’re nice, but this is a tech town. Skyscrapers would fill the entire peninsula. Instead of wealth taxes on billionaires, the city might even cut taxes to encourage more founders and companies to move there.

This is only a slight caricature of how city government works in China. Provincial cities like Hefei and Hangzhou have become world-leading centers of commerce in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, solar panels, batteries, and AI, steered by mayors whose career incentives are similar to those of partners in a venture capital firm, getting promoted if their portfolio grows and fired if it fails. The cities they run function as vertically integrated conglomerates that benefit not just from the success of their local champions, but also from the broader growth generated by masses of companies in their slipstream.

In the West, China’s success is often attributed to the central government’s willingness to pick winners and direct its economy from above. Many Westerners have concluded that a similar top-down approach is needed in their countries to create champions that can compete with China’s. But Beijing’s role is more akin to being a rulemaker in a great tournament. Subnational governments – provinces, cities, towns, villages – are responsible for around 85 percent of public expenditure, according to the IMF, the lion’s share of which is spent at city level.

The heavy state involvement correctly perceived by observers belongs not to Beijing but to those local governments, of which China has thousands, and which compete with one another for investment and prestige. These local growth machines and the competition between them are what drives China’s stunning economic success, and what the Western world must embrace to keep up.

Local heroes

For the initial decades after China’s economic opening in the 1980s, ‘Made in China’ meant cheap goods mass-produced for Western businesses. Today, Chinese companies lead the world in high-tech manufacturing, and many of them are household names in the West. Huawei is arguably the world’s most advanced telecoms company; BYD is the largest electric automaker; and DJI makes over 90 percent of consumer drones. Less familiar but no less important are companies like Geely, an auto giant which began in the 1980s as a refrigerator parts manufacturer and now owns Volvo, Lotus, Polestar and a stake in Aston Martin; and Vivo, now India’s biggest smartphone supplier.

What all have in common is that Beijing played no role in their creation. They were private companies encouraged by local governments. Huawei, BYD, and DJI emerged from Shenzhen’s Special Economic Zone, where municipal bureaucrats could write local regulations without regard for national rules. Geely was quietly supported by Zhejiang province at a time when only state-designated automakers were meant to build cars. Vivo spun off from a company founded in Dongguan, after Zhongshan, the neighboring city, wouldn’t give the company leaders equity.

Some sectors, such as batteries, electronics, and most recently electric vehicles, have received special support from Beijing as strategic industries. Companies in these areas benefited from subsidies, tax rebates, and in the case of electric cars, sales tax exemptions. But though the state was happy to lend its support to certain sectors, it was agnostic as to which specific firms and regions rose to dominance by means of that support. Beijing set a prize, and local bureaucrats competed to win it.

Hefei, the capital of Anhui province in inland Eastern China, is the most famous illustration of this process in action. In 2008, the municipal government invested $500 million in the electronic display company BOE Technology to build a new-generation LCD production line, bringing China to the cutting edge of panel production for the first time. At the time, Hefei was an unremarkable city with no display industry, and BOE was only the world’s ninth-largest manufacturer of LCD displays. The city provided the necessary land, utility connections, and cheap capital (investing almost a tenth of its total revenue that year) to set up a subsidiary company with BOE, in which it had an 81 percent stake. The bet paid off. BOE is now the world’s largest display panel manufacturer and makes about a quarter of smartphone screens worldwide.

The city reinvested the returns from its investment in other venture capital–like bets, which have won big surprisingly often. Hefei’s investment in carmaker NIO, which the city backed in 2020 in exchange for a 24 percent stake, paid off with an internal rate of return exceeding 30 percent. CXMT (Changxin Memory Technologies), 24 percent of which is directly or indirectly owned by the city of Hefei, runs just behind Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron with 7 percent of the global market for DRAM chips, the short-term memory used in smartphones, PCs, and data centers. Over the decade to 2023, the city had invested roughly $25 billion of public funds, generating reported earnings of nearly $9 billion.…

item.title: Victorian elites stayed in bed until the afternoon
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, interesting historical perspective

This is our third article from Issue 26, which arrives with print subscribers this week.

Books about successful people often make success sound rather unappealing. Education should be intense and rigorous, focused on driving up IQ and on the ‘STEM’ quaternity of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. Once adulthood is reached, life follows an austere pattern, with a 5am start, cold baths, daily visits to the gym, little or no alcohol, a Huel-rich diet, and Stakhanovite working hours. This last point generates particular excitement, and descriptions of powerful people dwell with eager fascination on how many hours they devote to their labors.

The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying. They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

Despite this, the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance. Its huge navy reigned over the world’s oceans, and its tiny army won a long sequence of wars while keeping watch over an enormous empire. Britain progressed gradually toward democracy with none of the revolutions and civil wars that wracked continental Europe. There is a longstanding view that the prosperity of Britain’s elites came at the cost of the hundreds of millions whom they subordinated and oppressed, and no doubt that is at least partly true. But on their own terms, the British ruling class enjoyed a victorious century.

Maybe the Victorian elite succeeded in spite of being feckless and incompetent: the Industrial Revolution created great wealth, which they enjoyed passively and parasitically. We cannot run controlled experiments on Victorian Britain, so this thesis is hard to test. But I want to explore the possibility that a relentless focus on soft skills, team building, and intra-elite networking actually worked rather well. Huel, STEM, and cold baths have their merits. But the example of the Victorians should make us hesitate before concluding that there is only one way to rule the world.

School

Caricaturing a little, we can distinguish two groups in modern educational debates: traditionalists and progressives. Traditionalists think that education should prioritize acquiring knowledge, that it should focus on ‘hard’ subjects like science, mathematics, and foreign languages, and that it should take place in a highly structured environment, where students’ time and behavior are tightly regulated. Progressives think that education should prioritize acquiring skills, that it should embrace ‘soft’ subjects beyond the supposed academic core, and that students should be given wide freedom in which to develop personally and socially.

One might assume that Victorian education was at the extreme traditionalist end of the spectrum, and modern educational progressives would indeed be horrified by the rote learning and corporal punishment of Victorian schooling. But in respect of all the controversies listed above, elite Victorian schools lean curiously toward the ‘progressive’ side of the spectrum.

Most socially elite Victorian boys began formal education at the age of seven or eight, spending about five years in a ‘preparatory school’ before passing on to a ‘public school’ (which, to the enduring confusion of international observers, is a kind of elite private school). There was a hierarchy of public schools, with the nine ‘Clarendon schools’ at the top, and just one, Eton College, clearly at the apex. About 30 percent of nineteenth-century cabinet ministers and 40 percent of prime ministers were Old Etonians.

Most students at both preparatory and public schools were boarders, meaning that elite Victorians were generally sent away from home by the age of eight and spent their childhoods more with peers than with family. In this respect they were distinctive even in their own time: elite families in continental Europe and the United States were far more likely to keep their children at home and educate them at small local private schools. It is plausible that this contributed to the lack of subnational loyalties in the British elite, in contrast to the distinct elites of, for example, the Southern United States, Catalonia in Spain, or Hungary in the Austrian Empire.

The public schools were of course single-sex, generating a somewhat febrile atmosphere in which intense quasi-romantic (or sometimes actually romantic) relationships between boys were common. Perhaps the powerful ties of nostalgia and loyalty that students felt for their former schoolmates were linked to this. The writer Jan Morris said that ‘the whole of English upper-class life…was shot through with bisexual instinct’ and that ‘the public school system…meant that male relationships were full of emotional nuance and undertone’. Demonstrative affection remained normal in adult life, and it was completely standard for pairs of Victorian men to walk arm-in-arm in public.…

item.title: how big (of) a problem?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

Tibs wrote to me in October 2020:

A few years ago, Americans started adding “of” in places it didn’t occur before. It gradually spread into books, and across the atlantic to here as well.

I don’t have an exact timing - less than 10 years?

I find it hard to remember examples, because it’s become part of the scenery, but it’s always a case where leaving out the “of” leaves the meaning identical

For instance: not that big [of] a deal ... as ordinary [of] a childhood as possible (this one from The Boys on Netflix)

My apologies, Tibs, for making you wait so long. Here we go!

What is it?

- an adverbial element (e.g., as, how, quite, so, this/that, too) that's indicating 'measurement' of the adjective

- a gradable adjective (i.e. the ones that can go with those 'measurement' expressions)

- of [which is not there in the older form]

- an indefinite noun phrase: usually one starting with a or an like an idea or a child; more unusually, you can find it with an indefinite (i.e. bare) plural or, even more rarely, a bare non-count noun [see examples 3 and 4 below, respectively].

- cacao provides habitat that is of as high of a quality as their natural forests (wisc.edu)

- Seems like I took too long of a break.(ER [tv])

- no matter how great their sacrifice or how big of heroes they might be (comment on a CNN blog)

- I asked him about how big of threat is ISIS to America's national security (CBS Face the Nation)

Why did people start saying it?

In analogical change, one pattern or piece of the language changes to become more like another pattern or piece of the language, where speakers perceive the changing part as similar to the pattern or piece that it changes to be more like. (2020: 87)

How much of a problem is that going to be? Too much of a problem.

When did people start saying it? And which people?

Harold Allen named The Big of Syndrome in the mid–late 1980s (he had died in 1988 before his [AmE linguist-speak] squib was published in American Speech). Allen had noticed expressions like this big of a crowd and that nice of a day ("an innovating syntactic aberration") in the Minnesota speech around him, and urged linguists to study it further. Linda Rapp took up the call and published another short article in 1991.

Rapp found several examples from 1943 in Harold Wentworth's 1944 American Dialect Dictionary. Wentworth's examples seem to be from West Virginia and central Florida. Another early-ish example (1962) comes from The Andy Griffith Show, which takes place in a (fictional) small town in North Carolina. So those seem like hints that it might have come from the inland southeast.

But since, unlike Rapp, I'm working in the Age of Linguistic Corpora, I've been able to find some earlier examples. These are from the Movie Corpus.

I had a quick look for the screenwriters' birthplaces—The Death Kiss = Alabama and Hungary and The Little Princess = California and Wisconsin. No one will admit to writing Lure of the Surf (which was apparently mocked for promoting sea fishing while sensible people were worried about U-boats), but the 'self-narrator' was from the Bronx. So, only one of those writers fits with the inland-southeast origin story. All of this is pointing to it being widespread in spoken American English even earlier. If people were saying it in (orig. AmE) movies without comment in the 1930s, it must have felt at least somewhat natural by then.

Still, before the 1980s, the corpus examples are few and far between. Allen wrote about the "syndrome" just as this pattern was finding real purchase in published English as well as spoken, with that big of a deal leading the way:

Tibs thought he'd only heard the pattern in the past decade. That could be due to Recency Illusion, or it could be that people in Britain just didn't hear it (or read it) much until the internet age. Sticking with big and deal (because the numbers are easiest to see), we can see it really taking off in the 2000s in published and performed American English. (Sorry, the text in these screenshots is not very clear, but know that the darker the blue, the more typical of a decade the phrase is. We can see big of a deal strongly associated with the 2000s, and much more so the 2010s. Neither of these corpora go into the 2020s.)

Just to underscore the Americanness of the expression: at the right end of the Movie Corpus screenshot, it shows that 145 of the examples came from a North American film. Only 4 came from British or Irish films.

Is it British yet?

The of has been coming to Britain, as Tibs noted. The table below shows how often big of a deal/difference occur per million words in the Corpus of Global Web-Based English (collected in 2012–13) and the News on the Web corpus (2010-now). In the news corpus, the BrE rate is 4 times lower than the AmE rate for each expression. The news data has a lot fewer of these expressions, presumably because the corpus has more professionally composed and edited text.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

A shorter (maybe), quicker and earlier post this month, since I am going to be travel(l)ing without much internet access in September and am (orig. AmE) freaking out* about how much work I have to do before the autumn/fall semester begins.

In a recent Language Log post, Victor Mair points out a difference in how American and British teens might react to this shirt:

Americans would tend to say I wouldn't be caught dead in it but BrE speakers would more likely say I wouldn't be seen dead in it.

To me, these bring up different images, since caught is a more dynamic verb than seen. Those who are caught are generally trying not to be caught. I wore the t-shirt, but I wanted to avoid being seen in it. But those who are seen can't help being seen. If you say 'I wouldn't be seen dead in it', it sounds to me like you fear someone putting the t-shirt on you after you've died. But maybe that difference in imagery is just me. Most people aren't so literalist about their idioms.

Anyhow...what's the history of these phrases? The OED has American caught dead from 1870 and American seen dead in 1887, then a Scottish-authored found dead in 1923, followed by British seen deads in the 1930s. So it's likely it started in the US, but then got translated a bit in UK.

Other 'be caught ADJECTIVE' phrases are also more American. (In this corpus result, the Token 1 column is number of hits in the US corpus, and the Token 2 column is UK).

So, generally, caught is used with adjectives to describe being in a situation you're not prepared for. With a noun, we also have caught by surprise (more than 2x more US hits in GloWbE).

But not all caught + adjective phrases with connotations of unreadiness are more American. Caught red-handed has more UK hits in the GloWbE corpus (less than 2x more), and that makes sense since red-handed is from Scotland in the early 1800s. (The red is the blood of the person you've just murdered.) That's a more literal caught, though—being caught by the police (or someone).

item.title: balk and baulk
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting topic, clear explanation

Over on Bluesky last month, I was pulled into a conversation that went something like this:

- Someone American asks "how long have y'all been adding a u to balk?"

- And then, predictably, some respondents say it's always been there, Noah Webster took it out.

The Oxford English Dictionary has it as balk. Since it comes from Old English, it only got a 'u' after French had influenced (I am tempted to say 'infected') the spelling system. The 'u' came into the word in the 1600s and 1700s, and today the spelling is very mixed in BrE. British National Corpus has 21 baulked/13 balked, more recent Corpus of Global Web-Based English has 71 baulked/93 balked in BrE. Cambridge, Chambers & Collins Dictionary all list balk first as does the Guardian Style Guide.

Most u/non-u variations in BrE and AmE involve an o—as in words like colo(u)r and mo(u)ld. The variation can probably be blamed on Samuel Johnson as much as Noah Webster. In the 18th-century, not all British dictionaries put a u in words like colo(u)r, but Johnson did, and his dictionary became far more famous than the others, so the u form eventually became standard in BrE. I write about the ou/o spellings at this old post (and much more and much better in in The Prodigal Tongue). But even Johnson spelled balk without the u.

My attention to the -o(u)- words in the book meant I overlooked balk/baulk—but I used the word balked in chapter 7:

...please seemed inappropriate in the small request situation, and so Americans balked at it.

The British copyeditor did not bat an eyelash—or a blue pencil—at it.

Given the dictionaries' agreement, we can say that balk is the "standard" spelling of the verb in BrE. Given the corpus numbers, we can say that it is the "normal" spelling. Given the word's history, we can say it is the "original" spelling.

But those corpus numbers aren't so distinct, and given the conversation on Bluesky, it seems that some BrE writers really want to spell it with a u (and to believe that that is the "standard/normal/original" way to spell it). This may well be another instance of British spelling changing in recent decades in order to fight against perceptions but not realities of a British/American spelling difference.*

Confusion about its spelling is understandable, though, since there is a noun that is more usually spelled/spelt baulk. It's part of a billiard-type game table, and the term is used in several terms in several such games.

I searched for several of these terms as either balk or baulk in Corpus of Global Web-Based English and got only the u spelling—with none of them in AmE:

(Britannica.com has it as balk. They're owned by the same company as Merriam-Webster. Is the ghost of Noah W. removing U's in the encyclop[a]edia?)

So, in general, if it's a [billiards] noun, it's baulk and if it's a verb it's balk. They both come from the same Old English word, with a Germanic ancestor.

The one other -aulk word in current English is caulk (used much more in AmE than BrE, which tends to say seal/sealant instead)—but that came into English with the u, as it came from French cauquer in the 1500s.

The post-Norman urge to stick a U in balk also affected talk and stalk in the 1600s, but not, apparently walk. For me, the mystery is: why has the urge to stick a U in persisted for baulk and not the others?

*I say 'another' instance of spelling change due to perceptions of 'Americanism' because I discuss the main instance of that phenomenon in detail in The Prodigal Tongue:

84 days, four titles, one historic feat - Alcaraz's remarkable return

The men's tennis season ended as it began, with a beaming Carlos Alcaraz holding aloft one of the sport's biggest trophies.

In January, he won the Australian Open to complete the career Grand Slam. Ten months later, he stood as the victor in Turin, having ended his wait for a first ATP Finals title.

Watching Alcaraz over recent weeks, it would be easy to forget that for a four-month period this year, the 23-year-old barely picked up a racquet.

He missed the majority of the clay and all of the grass-court season with a wrist injury, but he has made a remarkable return, culminating in a dismantling of world number one Alexander Zverev on Sunday.

It is 84 days since Alcaraz made his comeback at the US Open, where his lack of match fitness understandably showed. He came through the early rounds but lost a five-set quarter-final epic against Ben Shelton.

Since then, the Spaniard has won 21 of his 22 matches - including each of the past 14 - and captured titles at four of the five tournaments he has contested.

He continues to make history, too, becoming the youngest man to win all four Slams and the season-ending Finals.

This was the third straight tournament he has won, following victories at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters earlier in November, and he has now won his past nine matches against fellow top-10 players.

The former world number one, currently ranked third behind Zverev and Jannik Sinner, continues to make up for lost time as he seeks to quickly reassert himself at the top of the sport.

"I think everybody feels he's the number one," Alcaraz said, stressing each player in the game has to treat themselves that way.

"Me, Sascha [Zverev], Jannik [Sinner], [Ben] Shelton. Having that confidence in yourself is really important.

"But right now the number one is Sascha. He really deserves it."

- Alcaraz outplays Zverev for first ATP Finals triumph

Crowd-pleasing variety, devastating power and astonishing athleticism did not take long to return to Alcaraz's game.

Even with a heavily strapped left leg after injuring his hamstring on Wednesday, he could not be stopped by the world's top players in Turin.

That included Zverev, who this year rose to the top of the rankings for the first time after claiming his first two major titles and recording a tour-leading 69 match wins.

Alcaraz, already a seven-time Slam winner, feels his own growth in the mental side of the sport has taken him to a different level in recent months.

He has specifically pointed to the new sense of perspective he gained from his time away from tennis in inspiring his scintillating year-end form.

"The injury made me realise what's really important," Alcaraz said.

"It's not winning. It's just about playing tennis. I realised that it is a gift every time that I can step on the court and compete healthy.

"When you realise that, everything comes easier.

"I don't feel stressed most of the time. I think right now I'm more mature, or I feel that, on a tennis court, I'm facing the problems and difficult moments in a different way."

Alcaraz threw himself to the ground after ending his wait to win the season-ending tournament before racing into the stands to celebrate with his team and family.

It marked the 30th title of his career, drawing him level with rival Sinner and behind only men's record 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic (102) among active ATP players.

More could soon be around the corner - should he manage to stay injury-free.

Victory in Paris has left him two titles away from emulating Sinner and Djokovic by completing the career 'Golden Masters' - winning all nine Masters 1,000 events, the level of tournament below the Slams.

Should he achieve that next season in Canada and Shanghai, it would leave him only an Olympic singles gold away from completing the sport.

His main obstacle to achieving such dominance still appears to be Sinner, given Alcaraz's positive head-to-head against Zverev.

Italian Sinner has been absent with a knee issue since Wimbledon but is aiming to return, external at the Australian Open, where Alcaraz will defend his title in January.

"In today's final, I needed to put the three Cs - cabeza, corazon, cojones - that my grandpa always tells me I have to give every time I step on the court," Alcaraz said.

"The three Cs in English is head, heart and balls. Today, that was what it was about.

"Lifting this trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time. It means the world to me."

Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc clashes 'cannot continue' after Las Vegas GP with Frederic Vasseur to speak to drivers again

Sunday 22 November 2026 17:03, UK

Ferrari team boss Frederic Vasseur says he will hold further discussions with drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton after their latest tangle in the Las Vegas Grand Prix, admitting such incidents "cannot continue".

After costly clashes in Monza and Mexico City earlier this season, the Ferrari drivers came together when battling over sixth place with 12 laps to go on the Strip circuit in a race dominated by slip-streaming in which the leading runners were covered by a handful of seconds for most of the race.

Leclerc attempted to overtake Hamilton with a move down the inside of Turn Seven but made contact with the Briton, who was spun around. Stewards found Leclerc at fault and handed him a 10-second penalty, which dropped him to 10th place. Hamilton finished seventh.

In an unusually-strongly worded statement in Ferrari's post-race press release, Vasseur said: "For the second time in three races, something unacceptable has happened between our drivers, and this cannot continue.

"We sent a very clear message to both drivers in Brazil, and today during the race we told them to think about the team when racing each other.

"Of course, in this kind of race you cannot freeze the positions because, with the slipstream, if you slow down, the car behind will overtake you.

"But our drivers should have handled the situation differently, as other team-mates did both in front of and behind them.

"Charles knows he made a mistake and apologised, but that doesn't change the result."

Speaking to the written media after the race, Vasseur had said: "All the other teams, they were able to overtake each other 20 times during the race.

"[Kimi] Antonelli-[George] Russell, [Oscar] Piastri-[Lando] Norris, even Isack [Hadjar] overtook Max [Verstappen].

"Honestly, you can't imagine the frustration for me but, for more importantly, for all the guys at the [team]."

What will happen next?

The situation is increasingly frustrating for Vasseur given it was only three weeks ago that he had to resolve the fallout from a first-lap battle between the drivers that likely cost the team a one-two result in Mexico.

Vasseur brought Hamilton and Leclerc together to speak four days later ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, a meeting he said had "cleared the situation" and acted as "a good reset on the mindset" ahead of that weekend. The Frenchman added that they even "left my room joking together".

Immediately after Sunday's race in Las Vegas, the Ferrari team principal held an initial conversation with Leclerc having asked the Monegasque driver to see him before anything else.

Asked afterwards what they had talked about, Vasseur said: "It was not a discussion, I spoke!

"He apologised, he understands, but the result is there. That you do a mistake, you say 'it's my mistake, I'm sorry' but you did a mistake."

Asked what would happen next, Vasseur said: "I want to digest tonight [after the race] and we'll have to sit down tomorrow with both of them and to take a decision."

He added: "I want, once again, to have a discussion tomorrow. Also Charles will digest the situation and I think it's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race.

"I saw Charles a bit down and I told him what I wanted to say but I'd prefer to discuss with him tomorrow about it."

'It's not a matter of rules' - Vasseur insists 'respect' the key between team-mates

The Las Vegas incident has placed renewed focus on what Vasseur will do to try and bring his drivers definitively into line, with scrutiny growing on whether Ferrari will follow the lead of other teams, such as McLaren and Mercedes, and introduce more formal 'rules of engagement' for what is allowed when in team-mate combat.

Hamilton has called for clearer policies in recent months and said after Sunday's race that "hopefully in the background they eventually figure it out".

Vasseur, however, believes the chaotic nature of Sunday's race shows that clean driving between team-mates is all about respect rather than predefined agreements.

"Honestly, it's not a matter of rules," insisted Vasseur.

"What can you do differently except that you have to respect your team-mate? In this kind of race you have to overtake the car who is in front of you. You can't stay behind, it's completely unmanageable.

"It means you just have to do it with respect when it's your team-mate, to take less risk, perhaps to come side by side and to come back behind. But you can't put it on the paper. I think the race of today [Sunday] nobody would write a scenario like this. Nobody can imagine a race like this. It means they just have to act in a professional way.

"Today it was unprofessional."

AB de Villiers claims he is certain Australia tampered with the ball as far back as the first Test of their infamous 2018 series in South Africa.

The former South Africa batter was in the middle when Cameron Bancroft was caught by TV cameras using sandpaper in the third Test at Newlands in Cape Town.

Bancroft, Usman Khawaja and Chadd Sayers have all alleged sandpaper was used to tamper with the ball in the second Test at Gqerberha, formerly Port Elizabeth.

De Villiers set up South Africa’s six-wicket win in that Test to level the series at 1-1 with an unbeaten century in the first innings.

After biting his tongue during the unfolding drama, South Africa’s fourth highest Test run-scorer has entered the fray to say he has “no doubt” Australia’s premeditated cheating began even earlier.

“It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE [Port Elizabeth],” the 42-year-old said on his YouTube channel on Monday. “We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time.

“Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I’ve played a lot of cricket there. So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or nails ... I don’t care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew.”

In his memoir, Sabr, Khawaja wrote that all players were aware of Australia’s ball tampering in Cape Town, and his claims have been supported by Bancroft, Sayers and David Warner.

That version was rejected as “nonsense” by now-captain Pat Cummins, who was backed by fellow quick Josh Hazlewood. In 2021 the bowling group from the Cape Town Test issued a joint statement denying any prior knowledge that sandpaper had been taken onto the field to tamper with the ball during the South Africa tour.

De Villiers suggested it was implausible Australia’s bowlers were not aware, and was critical of their denials about the use of sandpaper on the field.

“Why are we all so worried about the object that was used?” he said. “The fact of the matter is there was a premeditated decision made to do something illegal on the ground.

“And every single person knew about it. I have zero per cent doubt about it.”

Cricket Australia declined to comment when contacted by Guardian Australia.

His most scathing criticism, however, was reserved for Cricket Australia’s handling of the fallout, and the team’s decision not to take collective responsibility at the time.

De Villiers said it was “absolutely ridiculous” Warner, Bancroft and then captain Steve Smith were left to take the hit and argued their suspensions were excessive.

“Cricket Australia needs to take the blame and not so much the players because they [CA] didn’t deal with it in the right manner,” he said. “It became a political thing. The prime minister [Malcolm Turnbull] got involved.

“The players obviously panicked. They were emotional ... I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later.”

De Villiers pointed to ball-tampering scandals of the 1990s involving England’s Michael Atherton and former South African captain Hansie Cronje as examples that were dealt with better.

Former South Africa captain Faf du Plessis was also found guilty by the ICC of ball tampering in 2013 and 2016, but was fined instead of suspended.

De Villiers admitted he wasn’t a “beautiful angel” over his career, but said he only engaged in legal methods to foster reverse swing, such as bouncing the ball on the pitch on return throws.

“We try and push the boundaries as much as possible,” he said. “We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object on to the field and blatantly cheating.”

item.title: OPINION: It’s time to put curiosity, creativity and critical thinking first in the early learning years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with original reporting

Early education is often judged by how quickly children master the 3 Rs: reading, writing and arithmetic. Those skills are essential, but not sufficient.

Children also need the 3 Cs: curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

We often treat the 3 Cs as “nice-to-haves” after children master reading, writing and arithmetic. But that gets the sequence backward.

Curiosity draws a child toward a book. Creativity links ideas in new ways as the child reads. Critical thinking helps the child assess whether those ideas fit together.

The 3 Cs are not a reward for finishing the academic work. Instead, they drive learning and make it stick.

Few educators would argue that the 3 Cs are unimportant. The problem is that we have organized early education around the 3 Rs. Further, our approach to these basic skills often reflects a predominantly academic style of teaching in the early years, with a proliferation of scripted curricula, worksheets, drills and questions with a single expected answer. I propose weaving the 3 Cs into early learning at school and at home through rich, back-and-forth conversations, open-ended questions and guided play.

In the early years, children learn what thinking feels like and discover with pride and excitement that they can generate their own ideas. Consider two pre-K classrooms:

In the first, a teacher asks, “Which block tower is taller?” An eager child gives the right answer, and the teacher moves to the next question.

In the second, the teacher asks, “Why did this block tower fall while the other one stayed up?” She waits and invites the class to test their explanations through guided play.

Both look like learning, but only the second engages the scientific method. By explaining, predicting, testing and reconsidering, children learn that ideas can improve.

At ages 4 and 5, children develop executive-function skills, including the capacity to focus, persist and organize their behavior. Kimberly Nesbitt and Dale Farran find that highly engaged, goal-directed and social classroom activities are associated with larger executive-function gains, especially for children entering pre-K with lower skills.

Rich conversations exercise language and self-regulation together.

Today, as AI makes answers easier to obtain, it is even more important for children to learn how to ask good questions and judge the answers they receive. Adults who can judge a machine’s output can delegate some cognitive work with little ill effect. But a 5-year-old is still developing that judgment; there is no shortcut to building it.

Curiosity develops by asking one question and learning that it leads to more questions. Creativity develops by generating possibilities and deciding which one clicks. Critical thinking develops by comparing claims against existing evidence.

Children strengthen these skills through active, repeated practice.

My research team observed 17 Chicago-area pre-K and kindergarten classrooms, examining the questions teachers asked and how they engaged children in conversation. Teachers asked closed-ended questions nearly three times as often as open-ended ones.

This was not due to indifference: All 21 teachers we interviewed called rich conversation very or extremely important. Most, however, had no training in effective language interactions with young children. Many cited time or uncertainty as barriers to initiating open-ended conversations.

Imagine a kindergarten teacher who wants to teach the word “oasis.” She shows a picture of a wet, green area in the desert and asks what children notice and why the oasis might exist. The children explore where the water comes from, how an oasis benefits nearby plants and animals and how often oases occur.

The children ask questions, offer explanations and build on one another’s ideas as they work toward understanding the unfamiliar word. In this approach, the child learns the word “oasis” and much more.

Related: TEACHER VOICE: Here’s why teachers should help students develop logic and reasoning skills early on

Teachers and parents bring distinct strengths to this approach. Teachers can connect open-ended conversations to lesson plans and provide children with repeated opportunities to reason with classmates. Parents know the child’s experiences, interests, language and ways of expressing ideas. During ordinary moments at home with a parent or caregiver, a child can revisit the topic in a familiar setting, expand on it and connect it to daily life.

When teachers and parents reinforce this approach together, children encounter the 3 Cs in the two places where they spend most of their early years.

Most school-family messaging platforms focus on logistics. A genuine family-school connection looks different. A teacher giving a physics lesson relays a request to parents: “Ask your child where her shadow goes.” The parent reports that her daughter noticed that her shadow changed length as they walked past a streetlight.

The teacher jump-starts the next morning’s class discussion with that answer, opening a new conversation about how light travels in straight lines. The child’s idea travels from school to home and back again, growing richer along the way.

This approach matters most for children with the fewest opportunities for rich conversations. It takes attention more than expertise.

A parent unsure how to talk about shadows does not need a crash course in the physics of light. That parent needs one good question and a willingness to listen sincerely to the child’s response.

There are resources to help. In our research lab, for example, we developed the adult-facing Chat2Learn tool, which gives teachers and parents open-ended prompts to start rich conversations.

We should continue teaching the 3 Rs directly and well. But we should stop treating curiosity, creativity and critical thinking as ancillary to the “real work” of reading, writing and arithmetic.…
